newsitem.title: GUAM: Investigators say no engine failure in Guam crash.
newsitem.headline: Investigators say no engine failure in Guam crash.

text.p: The Korean Air Lines jumbo jet that ploughed into a hilltop while attempting to land on this Pacific island did not suffer any engine or structural failure before crashing, U.S. investigators said on Friday.

The investigators from the National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) also said the crew were apparently not aware of any problem as the aircraft approached the island's main airport in the dark during a heavy rainstorm.

Also on Friday, nine Taiwanese monks and nuns were flown to Guam and held a Buddhist memorial service for about 50 members of the victims' families. The mourners wailed, chanted and burned incense during the service at a makeshift alter near the crash site with the tail section of the airplane visible in the background.

George Black, leader of the NTSB team investigating the crash, said at a news conference that the cause of the crash was far from being determined, while KAL defended itself against a media report that blamed pilot error for the crash.
Black also discounted media reports that officials had tentatively concluded pilot error was to blame.
"Those reports are pure speculation and are based on things that we have not even looked at," he said.

Twenty-nine of the 254 people on board KAL Flight 801 survived the crash, Black said, contradicting the figure of 27 given earlier by Korean Air Lines and military officials. Black said he could not account for the discrepancy.
The U.S. TV network NBC "Nightly News" on Thursday quoted unidentified sources as saying the initial analysis of the recorders showed the crash was caused by pilot error.
It said the pilots apparently homed in on a radio signal on a hilltop three miles (five km) from the airport, mistakenly believing they were homing in on the runway.
They then made a straight descent on to the hillside, and lowered the landing gear before impact, disabling the alarm system that would have warned them of the impending crash, NBC said.
In a statement issued in Seoul, KAL said such conclusions were too hasty.

"We are not yet ruling out the possibility of a sudden change in altitude caused by torrential rains, the breakdown of the glide slope or other elements, which combined, could have caused the accident," KAL said.

The glide slope, a portion of a landing instrument that guides the planes to the runway, has been out of service, according to Guam officials, and KAL acknowledges it had been notified and was aware of the absence of the instrument.

Investigators have recovered half of the bodies from the wreckage of the Boeing 747, scattered over hilly jungle terrain in sight of the runway and below a crest near a guidance beacon. The fuselage had been broken into four section.
"Half of all the passengers and crew have been found and removed," said Matt Furman, an NTSB official.
The flight recorders were virtually undamaged and could hold clues to the cause of the crash, U.S. officials said.
"Both are in excellent shape; the tapes are in good shape. There is useful data from both the black boxes," Dr Vernon Ellingstad, director of research and engineering at the NTSB told reporters.
The NTSB's Furman was speaking to about 200 members of mostly South Korean families who had relatives on Flight 801.

"There has been a misunderstanding that the removal of your loved ones has stopped and that is not true. We are constantly removing the bodies, but I want you to understand that the work is very hard and dangerous because of the heat and terrain," Furman said.

Furman repeated assurances that the bodies were being taken out as quickly as possible. "More than 100 U.S. military personnel are working under dangerous conditions. We have not stopped the process and anything other than this that you may have heard is not true."

Officials from KAL, Boeing, engine makers Pratt and Whitney, the U.S. Federal Aviation Administration, the FBI and the NTSB were working together in the investigation that could take more than a year, Furman said.
A Korean doctor said on Friday that survivors of the crash have shown great mental strength amid the anguish felt for their dead loved ones,
"All of those we've treated are incredibly strong mentally, especially considering their experience and their loss," said Dr Moon G. Yoon of Guam Memorial Hospital.
